screens.title: Inheritance Fundamentals and the super Keyword
screens.subtitle: Reuse behavior, form 'is-a' hierarchies, and chain constructors safely

narration.text: Today we explore inheritance in Java and the super keyword, two features that let you build cleaner, more reusable class hierarchies. Inheritance allows a class to acquire fields and methods from another class, creating an “is-a” relationship: a Car is a Vehicle, a Circle is a Shape. You will see why that matters: common code lives once in a superclass and is reused by many subclasses, making programs easier to extend and maintain. The super keyword performs two vital roles: it calls a superclass constructor to initialize inherited state, and it gives a subclass a way to access the superclass implementation when names are hidden or methods are overridden. We will study constructor chaining — how constructors execute up the chain — and common pitfalls such as a missing no-argument constructor or attempts to access private fields directly from subclasses. Concrete examples use Vehicle and Car, and a hands-on Shape/Circle exercise will let you practice calling super and overriding a method while still using the parent’s behavior. By the end of this lesson you will understand what inheritance gives you, when to use it, and how super keeps initialization correct. Consider: when you design a new class, which parts belong in a shared parent and which belong only to the specialized child?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Inheritance reuses fields and methods through an is-a relationship; super ensures proper constructor calls and access to parent implementations.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Inheritance & super
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Inheritance Fundamentals

Learn how subclasses acquire behavior from superclasses, how to call parent constructors, and how to avoid common pitfalls.

In this lesson
Inheritance • extends • super • Constructor chaining
Why it matters

Shared behavior lives in one place. When Vehicle provides accelerate and brake, every subclass can reuse that code without duplication.

What you'll practice

Create subclasses with extends, call super(...) in constructors, and override methods while calling the parent implementation when needed.

Illustration

A small card cluster shows Vehicle as the parent with Car and Motorcycle as children. Each child reuses speed and brand, adding its own fields like numberOfDoors.

Vehicle{brand, speed} ↦ accelerate(), brake()
Car extends Vehicle {numberOfDoors, honk()}
Coming up: constructor chaining example and a Shape/Circle coding exercise.
Explore Key Topics
extends keyword

Declares that a class inherits from another. Example: class Car extends Vehicle.

super keyword

Calls the parent constructor or accesses the parent implementation when needed.

Constructor chaining

Constructors run up the inheritance chain so parent state is initialized before child-specific setup.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives map directly to the skills you'll practice. First, you will be able to define inheritance in Java and explain how it creates an is-a relationship between classes. That definition includes why code reusability and extensibility follow when shared behavior lives in a superclass. Second, you'll use the extends keyword to construct subclasses that reuse superclass members; you'll see the exact syntax and the rule that a class can extend only one other class. Third, you'll analyze how subclass objects inherit fields and methods and how access modifiers, especially private, affect what a subclass can directly access. Finally on this screen, you'll practice using super to call a parent constructor and to reference a parent's implementation when a subclass overrides a method. Each objective includes a short mnemonic so you can remember the skill during coding. These outcomes prepare you to read and write simple inheritance hierarchies, avoid common mistakes like forgetting to call a required superclass constructor, and reason about when to place behavior in a parent class versus a child.

screens.title: What is inheritance?
screens.subtitle: A precise definition, benefits, and a working example

narration.text: Inheritance is a language-level mechanism where a class acquires properties and behaviors from another class. In Java we say a subclass inherits from a superclass. This creates an is-a relationship: a Car is-a Vehicle. The key benefits are code reusability and extensibility. Reusability means common fields and methods live once in the superclass instead of being duplicated across many classes. Extensibility means you can add subclass-specific fields or methods without modifying the superclass, which keeps the original class stable. For a concrete example, the Vehicle class can define brand and speed plus accelerate and brake. When Car extends Vehicle, a Car object already has speed and accelerate available; the Car class adds numberOfDoors and a honk method. A common misconception is that inheritance automatically exposes private fields; it does not. Private fields remain accessible only inside their owning class; subclasses should use public or protected getters and setters to interact with that state. Another confusion is mixing inheritance with composition; inheritance establishes an is-a relationship and is best used when that conceptual fit is clear. Takeaway: use inheritance to share common behavior and state when a true is-a relationship exists, and always manage access to parent fields through controlled interfaces.

keyIdea.title: Definition takeaway
keyIdea.text: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse fields and methods from a superclass, forming an is-a relationship and promoting reuse.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › What is inheritance?
Definition

Inheritance

Inheritance is a mechanism where one class acquires fields and methods from another, creating an is-a relationship and enabling reuse.

Benefit: Code Reusability

Write a method once in the superclass and reuse it in many subclasses.

Benefit: Extensibility

Add specialized behavior in subclasses without changing the shared parent.

Common misconception

Inheritance does not grant direct access to private fields; use getters or protected members instead.

Key Takeaway

Use inheritance when a clear is-a relationship exists and you want to share behavior across related classes.

Concrete example

Vehicle and Car

// Superclass
public class Vehicle {
  private String brand;
  private int speed;
  public void accelerate(int increment) { /* update speed */ }
}

// Subclass
public class Car extends Vehicle {
  private int numberOfDoors;
  public void honk() { /* Car-specific */ }
}
Analogy

Think of a superclass as a blueprint for shared features and a subclass as a specialized blueprint that adds its own parts.

screens.title: Using extends to make a subclass
screens.subtitle: Syntax, single inheritance rule, and a code example

narration.text: In Java, the extends keyword declares that one class inherits from another. The syntax is concise: class Child extends Parent. Java supports single inheritance of classes, so a class may extend only one direct superclass. In practice this means you must design which class will hold shared behavior or rely on interfaces for additional contracts. Consider the provided Vehicle and Car example: when you write public class Car extends Vehicle, Car automatically has the Vehicle fields and methods unless they are private. The code snippet in the lesson shows a Vehicle constructor that initializes brand and a Car constructor that calls super(brand). Remember: if Vehicle has no no-argument constructor, the Car constructor must explicitly call a matching superclass constructor as its first statement. A common mistake is to assume you can call super(...) after other statements; the compiler requires it first. Also avoid trying to extend multiple concrete classes; instead use interfaces for additional behavior. Practically, use extends when a true is-a relationship exists and you want the child to reuse the parent's implementation. Try writing a small subclass and observe which methods you can call without adding them again.

keyIdea.title: Syntax tip
keyIdea.text: Use class Child extends Parent; always ensure required superclass constructors are called when needed.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Using extends
Syntax

class Subclass extends Superclass

Extends creates a direct parent-child link. A class may extend only one other class in Java.

public class Vehicle {
  private String brand;
  public Vehicle(String brand) { this.brand = brand; }
}

public class Car extends Vehicle {
  public Car(String brand, int doors) {
    super(brand); // must be first
    // initialize doors
  }
}
Common mistake

Calling super(...) after other statements in the constructor causes a compile-time error.

Pro tip

If you need multiple behaviors, prefer interfaces rather than attempting multiple class inheritance.

Example in action

Creating a Car instance calls Vehicle's constructor to initialize brand, then runs Car-specific initialization for doors. The Car object then can call accelerate or getBrand without reimplementing those methods.

Scenario

Imagine you have many vehicle types; putting common behavior in Vehicle prevents repeating accelerate, brake, and brand logic in every subclass.

Key Takeaway

Use extends for clear is-a relationships and always match superclass constructors when needed.

screens.title: What subclasses inherit
screens.subtitle: Fields, methods, and the role of access modifiers

narration.text: A subclass inherits the accessible fields and methods declared in its superclass. That generally includes public and protected members and package-private members when in the same package. Private fields are not directly accessible to subclasses; they remain encapsulated inside the superclass. In practice this means a subclass can call inherited public methods like getBrand() or accelerate(), but it should not attempt to read a private field directly. The Vehicle/Car example shows brand and speed stored in Vehicle, with Car using getBrand() to print the brand. A frequent misconception is to think inheritance automatically allows direct field sharing; encapsulation still applies. Another important point is that inheritance brings behavior: if the superclass provides an implementation for a method, the subclass automatically has that behavior unless it overrides the method. Overriding replaces the inherited implementation but can still call the parent version via super. methodName(). Concrete example: getBrand() implemented in Vehicle is available to Car and used inside Car's honk method. Takeaway: inheritance gives access to behavior and accessible state but preserves encapsulation rules, so use getters and protected access intentionally. What subclasses inherit means subclasses gain access to public and protected members and inherit method implementations, but private fields remain private to the superclass.. In practical terms, fields, methods, and the role of access modifiers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Inheritance detail
keyIdea.text: Subclasses gain access to public and protected members and inherit method implementations, but private fields remain private to the superclass.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › What subclasses inherit
Comparison

Inherited vs. not inherited

Inherited
  • public and protected methods
  • public fields (if present)
  • method implementations
Not directly inherited
  • private fields and private methods
  • constructor bodies (but constructors run through chaining)
Practical rule

Use getters or protected modifiers when the subclass needs access to parent data; keep fields private to preserve encapsulation unless subclass access is necessary.

Key Takeaway

Inheritance shares behavior, not the right to break encapsulation. Use controlled access to parent state.

Concrete example
public class Vehicle {
  private String brand;
  public String getBrand() { return brand; }
}

public class Car extends Vehicle {
  public void honk() {
    System.out.println(getBrand() + " says Beep!");
  }
}
Misconception

Don't assume inherited fields are accessible directly; use the superclass's getters to respect encapsulation and avoid errors.

screens.title: The super keyword: constructor calls and member access
screens.subtitle: How super(...) and super.methodName() work in practice

narration.text: The super keyword serves two connected purposes. First, super(...) calls a superclass constructor from a subclass constructor to initialize inherited state. That call must be the very first statement in the subclass constructor. If the superclass offers only parameterized constructors, you must explicitly call one of them with super(...) or the code will fail to compile. Second, super. methodName() or super. fieldName (when allowed) accesses a superclass member directly, which is useful when a subclass overrides a method but still needs the original behavior. For example, if Shape has displayInfo and Circle overrides it to print radius, Circle can call super. displayInfo() to reuse the parent’s info before adding its own. A typical misconception is that super can access private fields; it cannot. Use super to call public or protected members of the parent. Also do not confuse calling super() with invoking parent methods on an instance reference; super is a compile-time keyword that refers to the immediate superclass implementation. Takeaway: use super to ensure parent initialization and to combine parent behavior with subclass-specific behavior safely. The super keyword: constructor calls and member access means super(...) initializes parent state; super.methodname() calls the parent's implementation when overriding.. In practical terms, how super(...) and super.methodname() work in practice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: super summary
keyIdea.text: super(...) initializes parent state; super.methodName() calls the parent's implementation when overriding.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › The super keyword
Usage

super(...) and super.method()

Super ensures inherited state is initialized and lets a subclass call the parent implementation when needed.

public class Vehicle {
  public Vehicle(String brand) { /* init */ }
  public void display() { System.out.println("Vehicle display"); }
}

public class Car extends Vehicle {
  public Car(String brand) {
    super(brand);
  }
  @Override
  public void display() {
    super.display(); // call parent behavior
    System.out.println("Car details");
  }
}
Misconception

super does not bypass access rules; private members of the parent remain inaccessible to the child.

Concrete example

When Car's constructor calls super(brand), Vehicle's constructor runs first to set brand. Later calls to super.display() let Car reuse the Vehicle display code and then add Car-specific output.

Pro tip

When overriding a method, call super.methodName() if you want to keep the parent's behavior and extend it, rather than replace it entirely.

Key Takeaway

Use super to initialize parent state and to combine parent and child behavior during overrides.

screens.title: Constructor chaining
screens.subtitle: How constructors run up the inheritance chain

narration.text: Constructor chaining is the ordered process by which constructors execute from the top of the hierarchy down to the most specific subclass. When you create a Car, Java ensures Vehicle's constructor runs first to initialize shared fields, then Car's constructor runs to set subclass-specific fields. If a subclass constructor does not explicitly call a superclass constructor, Java inserts an implicit call to super() as the first statement; that implicit call requires the superclass to have a no-argument constructor. If it does not, you must explicitly call super(...) with matching parameters. A concrete example is the Animal and Dog snippet: Animal has a constructor Animal(String name). Dog must call super(name) as its first line, otherwise compilation fails. A common error is to try assigning to the superclass's private fields from the subclass instead of calling the appropriate constructor or using setters. Constructor chaining preserves object invariants by guaranteeing that parent initialization completes before child initialization begins. Takeaway: always ensure your subclass constructors invoke appropriate superclass constructors so every part of the object is initialized in the correct order. Constructor chaining means constructors execute from parent to child; explicit super(...) is required if the parent lacks a no-argument constructor.. In practical terms, how constructors run up the inheritance chain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Chaining rule
keyIdea.text: Constructors execute from parent to child; explicit super(...) is required if the parent lacks a no-argument constructor.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Constructor chaining
Steps
1. Call new Subclass(...)
2. Subclass constructor executes; first statement is super(...) or implicit super()
3. Superclass constructor runs and initializes parent state
4. Control returns to subclass constructor to finish initialization
Key Takeaway

Constructor chaining ensures the parent initializes before the child; explicit super(...) is required when no default parent constructor exists.

Concrete example
class Animal {
  private String name;
  public Animal(String name) { this.name = name; }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
  private String breed;
  public Dog(String name, String breed) {
    super(name); // required
    this.breed = breed;
  }
}
Common error

If you omit the explicit super(name) and Animal has no no-arg constructor, compilation fails because the implicit super() does not exist.

screens.title: Common pitfalls when using inheritance
screens.subtitle: Missing super calls, private fields, and incorrect assumptions

narration.text: Working with inheritance introduces a small set of repeated mistakes that are easy to avoid once you recognize them. One common pitfall is forgetting to call a required superclass constructor. If the superclass only provides parameterized constructors, failing to call super(...) as the first line in your subclass constructor produces a compile error. Another mistake is trying to access private fields of the superclass directly; private members are not inherited in the sense of direct access and must be reached via getters or protected fields. A third error is assuming a superclass reference has subclass-specific methods. For example, creating a Vehicle reference to a Car object lets you call accelerate(), but not honk(), because honk() is not part of Vehicle’s A P I. That mismatch is a common source of confusion for beginners. A final practical trap is attempting multiple class inheritance; Java prevents this and requires interfaces for multiple contracts. The safe pattern is to check the parent’s constructors and A P I before extending it, and to expose controlled accessors when subclasses legitimately need state from the parent. Question to reflect on: when is inheritance the right tool, and when might composition be preferable?

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls summary
keyIdea.text: Avoid missing super calls, respect private fields, and do not assume superclass references expose subclass-specific methods.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Common pitfalls
Error patterns

Frequent mistakes

  • Omitting explicit super(...) when the superclass lacks a no-argument constructor.
  • Attempting to access private superclass fields directly instead of using getters.
  • Expecting a superclass reference to expose subclass-specific methods like honk().
  • Trying to extend multiple concrete classes — Java disallows it.
Check your code

Always confirm the parent constructors and available methods before extending a class to prevent compile-time surprises.

Concrete scenario
Car myCar = new Car("Toyota", 4);
Vehicle v = myCar;
v.accelerate(50); // OK - defined in Vehicle
// v.honk(); // Compile-time error - honk is not in Vehicle's API
Reflect

Which classes in your codebase really form an is-a relationship, and which should instead be composed?

screens.title: Shape and Circle: a step-by-step implementation
screens.subtitle: Follow the activity to practice super and overriding

narration.text: This hands-on activity guides you through implementing a Shape superclass and a Circle subclass so you can practice calling super, overriding methods, and calculating derived values. Start by creating Shape with private fields color and isFilled, a constructor Shape(String color, boolean isFilled), getters for both fields, and a displayInfo method that prints color and filled status. Next implement Circle extends Shape with a private radius field and a constructor Circle(String color, boolean isFilled, double radius) that calls super(color, isFilled) as its first statement. Add a public getter for radius and a getArea method that returns Math. PI * radius * radius. Finally override displayInfo in Circle, but call super. displayInfo() first to show the base information, then print radius and area. A common misconception is to override displayInfo without calling super, which loses the shared information printed by the parent. After implementing these methods, create a DrawingApp main that constructs both a Shape and a Circle, calls displayInfo on each, and prints the circle area. This sequence demonstrates constructor chaining, proper use of super, and how overriding can augment rather than replace parent behavior.

keyIdea.title: Exercise goal
keyIdea.text: Implement Shape and Circle to practice constructor chaining, super calls, getters, overriding, and area calculation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Shape / Circle Exercise
Starter code
// Shape.java
public class Shape {
  private String color;
  private boolean isFilled;

  // TODO: Implement the constructor Shape(String color, boolean isFilled)
  // TODO: Implement public getter methods for color and isFilled

  public void displayInfo() {
    System.out.println("Shape Color: " + this.color + ", Filled: " + (this.isFilled ? "Yes" : "No"));
  }
}

// Circle.java
public class Circle extends Shape {
  private double radius;

  // TODO: Implement the constructor Circle(String color, boolean isFilled, double radius)
  // Remember to call the superclass constructor!

  // TODO: Implement public getter method for radius
  // TODO: Implement public double getArea() method

  @Override
  public void displayInfo() {
    super.displayInfo(); // Call the superclass's displayInfo method
    // TODO: Print Circle-specific info (radius and area)
  }
}
Implementation hints
  • Call super(color, isFilled) as the first statement in Circle's constructor.
  • Calculate area with Math.PI * radius * radius.
  • Use super.displayInfo() inside overridden displayInfo to preserve base output.
Expected behavior

When you run DrawingApp, Shape.displayInfo should print color and filled status. Circle.displayInfo should first print the same info via super.displayInfo and then print radius and computed area.

Check your understanding

If Circle.displayInfo omits super.displayInfo, what shared information will be missing from the output?

Key Takeaway

Implement constructors and overrides so parent state is initialized and parent behavior can be reused via super.

screens.title: How inheritance prepares for polymorphism
screens.subtitle: Why shared superclasses let objects be treated uniformly

narration.text: Although polymorphism is covered in the next module, understanding how inheritance sets it up is essential. When subclasses share a common superclass, you can treat different subclass instances as instances of the superclass type. For example, a Car assigned to a Vehicle reference still uses Vehicle's public A P I, so accelerate and brake remain callable. This uniform treatment is what enables polymorphic behavior later: different subclasses can supply different implementations of a shared method and be used interchangeably through their common type. A common contrast students make is confusing the compile-time type and run-time type: the compile-time type (the declared reference) determines which methods the compiler allows you to call. The run-time type (the actual object) determines which overridden implementation executes. Concrete example from earlier: Vehicle genericVehicle = new Vehicle("Bicycle") cannot call honk(), but Vehicle v = new Car("Toyota", 4) can call accelerate(), and at run time the Car's implementation will execute if accelerate is overridden. Takeaway: inheritance is the scaffolding that makes polymorphism possible, but A P I design in the superclass determines what clients can call. How inheritance prepares for polymorphism means inheritance groups related classes under a common type so they can be used interchangeably through that type's api.. In practical terms, why shared superclasses let objects be treated uniformly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Polymorphism prep
keyIdea.text: Inheritance groups related classes under a common type so they can be used interchangeably through that type's API.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Inheritance → Polymorphism
Concept link

Shared type enables interchange

When subclasses share a superclass, code can work with the common type and accept many concrete forms later, which is the basis for polymorphism.

Example

Vehicle v = new Car("Toyota", 4); v.accelerate(50); The compiler checks Vehicle's API, and the runtime uses the Car behavior if accelerate was overridden.

Key Takeaway

Design superclass APIs with the methods clients need so polymorphism becomes practical and safe.

Contrast

Remember the distinction between compile-time type (what the code can call) and run-time type (which implementation actually runs). Confusing these leads to mistaken expectations about available methods.

Reflective question

If you need to call a subclass-specific method, should client code refer to the subclass type or the superclass type? Why?

screens.title: Practical guidelines and best practices
screens.subtitle: When to put behavior in a superclass and how to avoid fragile hierarchies

narration.text: Inheritance is powerful, but applied badly it can make code brittle. Place shared, stable behavior in a superclass—things that are unlikely to change across subclasses. Avoid putting very specific behavior into a widely used parent because changing it affects all children. Prefer protected or public accessors to expose necessary parent state rather than making fields public or trying to reach private fields directly. Remember Java’s single-class inheritance rule: if you need multiple capabilities, use interfaces to add contracts without introducing fragile coupling. Another helpful guideline is to favor composition when the relationship is not truly is-a; for example, if a class uses features of another class but is not a subtype conceptually, composition keeps responsibilities clear. The chapter emphasizes constructor chaining and super usage: always ensure your constructors call required parent constructors to initialize inherited fields. A simple test after refactoring is to create instances of each subclass and verify initialization and behavior still work. Takeaway: design inheritance intentionally, expose minimal necessary parent state, and use super only to combine or initialize parent behavior safely. Practical guidelines and best practices means keep inheritance focused on stable shared behavior, prefer accessors to direct field exposure, and use interfaces or composition when inheritance does not fit.. In practical terms, when to put behavior in a superclass and how to avoid fragile hierarchies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design summary
keyIdea.text: Keep inheritance focused on stable shared behavior, prefer accessors to direct field exposure, and use interfaces or composition when inheritance does not fit.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Design Guidance
Practical rules

Keep hierarchies intentional

Shared, stable behavior

Place commonly used operations in the superclass to avoid duplication.

Expose via accessors

Use getters or protected methods rather than exposing fields directly.

Prefer interfaces/composition

When a class needs multiple behaviors or is not a subtype conceptually, prefer interfaces or composition.

Quick checklist
  • Does the child truly satisfy an is-a relation with the parent?
  • Are parent constructors reachable and called correctly?
  • Are private fields accessed only through getters?
Key Takeaway

Design hierarchies intentionally, keep parent state encapsulated, and call super constructors to maintain correct initialization order.

narration.text: Let's consolidate the chapter into a short list of key concepts to remember. First, inheritance is the mechanism where one class acquires fields and methods of another, forming an is-a relationship that promotes reuse and extensibility. Second, the superclass or parent class is the source of shared behavior, while the subclass or child class is the specialized type that extends it. Third, the extends keyword declares the inheritance relationship in Java — for example class Car extends Vehicle — and Java allows only single inheritance of classes. These core items form the vocabulary you need to read and reason about class hierarchies. Keep these in mind as you design types: look for true is-a relationships and prefer to place shared, stable behavior in the parent class. A final reflective question: when you see a repeated piece of behavior across classes, ask whether it belongs in a shared superclass.

keyIdea.title: Quick memory
keyIdea.text: Inheritance, superclass, subclass, and extends are the vocabulary for building class hierarchies and sharing behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts
Inheritance
A mechanism where a subclass acquires fields and methods from a superclass.
Superclass (Parent)
The class that defines shared fields and methods used by subclasses.
Subclass (Child)
A class that extends a superclass and may add fields or methods.
Summary

These concepts form the foundation for shared behavior and polymorphism in object-oriented design.

narration.text: Finish by remembering the practical keywords and rules you will use in code. The extends keyword establishes inheritance in Java — class Child extends Parent — and Java does not allow a class to extend more than one other class. The super keyword has two main roles: calling a parent constructor and invoking a parent's method implementation from a subclass. Finally, constructor chaining is the process by which constructors run: parent constructors execute before child constructors so inherited state is initialized correctly. Keep these short rules in mind when you design hierarchies and write constructors. A quick question to keep: when you see a superclass without a no-argument constructor, what must each subclass constructor include? The answer is an explicit call to an appropriate super(...) constructor as the first statement.

keyIdea.title: Practical rules
keyIdea.text: Use extends to declare inheritance, use super to initialize and access parent behavior, and call superclass constructors to maintain correct initialization order.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts
extends
Keyword used to declare a subclass relationship between classes.
super
Calls a superclass constructor or a superclass method implementation from a subclass.
Constructor chaining
The ordered execution of constructors up the inheritance hierarchy so parent state initializes first.
Final takeaway

Remember these rules and check parent constructors before subclassing; use super to preserve correct initialization and access parent behavior.
